notes.meaning: The heavenly guide brings Ezekiel into the main hall of the temple, called the Holy Place or outer sanctuary. He measures the massive doorposts on each side of the entrance to be about ten and a half feet wide. Together, these two thick posts equal the entire width of Moses' ancient wilderness tent, showing how grand and solid this new building is.

differ.view: These detailed room dimensions describe a literal, physical temple that will be built in Jerusalem in the future.
The vision uses earthly temple language to symbolize the perfect spiritual dwelling of God among His people in Christ and the church.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic interpretation traditionally sees the vision as looking partly to the second temple after the exile, but fully fulfilled in the spiritual reality of the Church.

notes.meaning: The entrance opening itself measures seventeen and a half feet wide, framed by walls nearly nine feet wide on either side. Inside, the main hall is seventy feet long and thirty-five feet wide. These measurements match the Holy Place in Solomon's temple, showing continuity with God's earlier dwelling among His people.

The guide goes ahead alone into the innermost room while Ezekiel waits outside. Ezekiel was a priest, but Old Testament law allowed only the high priest to enter this most sacred room, and only once a year. The guide measures the inner doorway and finds it narrower than the outer entrance, showing that holiness demands greater reverence as one comes nearer to God.

The guide measures the inner room and finds it to be thirty-five feet long and thirty-five feet wide. He tells Ezekiel that this room is the Most Holy Place, where God's presence rests. Because it forms a perfect square, just like the Holy of Holies in Solomon's temple, it reflects God's complete perfection and unchanging stability.

The guide then measures the main wall of the temple and finds it to be ten and a half feet thick. Along the outside of this massive wall are side rooms that are seven feet wide. These rooms served as secure spaces to store priestly garments, sacred dishes, and tithes given to God.

The side rooms are built in three levels of thirty rooms each, making ninety rooms in all. The rooms rest on ledges in the temple wall rather than being fixed directly into it, preserving the wall from damage. Each story is wider than the one below it because the outer temple wall narrows as it goes up, and a winding staircase connects the three floors.

differ.view: The side rooms widening as they ascend represent the church growing larger and more glorious as it draws closer to heaven.

notes.meaning: Ezekiel notices that the whole temple building rests on a raised stone platform about ten and a half feet high. The outer wall of the side rooms is nearly nine feet thick, giving the rooms great strength and protection. Outside these rooms is an open walkway where priests could move along the building.

An open courtyard thirty-five feet wide runs around the building, separating the side rooms from the outer court chambers. The side rooms open out onto an eight-and-a-half-foot walkway, with one door facing north and another facing south. This open space kept the temple building distinct and honored as holy ground.

A large separate building stands behind the temple on the west side, measuring about one hundred and twenty feet wide and over one hundred and fifty feet long. Its walls are nearly nine feet thick all around. This building helped guard the back of the temple, ensuring that no unauthorized person could approach the holy presence from behind.

The guide measures the full length of the temple structure from east to west and finds it to be one hundred cubits, or about one hundred and seventy-five feet. The front of the temple along the eastern court also measures one hundred cubits wide. The equal length and breadth highlight the balanced order and harmony of God's house.

The guide measures the western building and its galleries, which also extend one hundred cubits. Inside the temple, all the walls, doorposts, and narrow windows are completely covered with wood paneling from the floor up. Measuring each section shows that nothing in God's dwelling is left to chance or disorder.

The wooden wall panels are carved with repeating patterns of cherubim and palm trees. Each cherub is shown with two faces, a human face looking toward one palm tree and a young lion face looking toward another. These carvings cover every wall from the floor to above the doorways, displaying God's majesty and the life and victory He gives His people.

The doorframes of the main sanctuary are rectangular and flat rather than arched. The entrance leading into the Most Holy Place has the exact same square design. This gives both sacred doorways a matching and dignified appearance.

Inside the room stands a wooden altar about five feet high and three and a half feet square. The guide calls it "the table that is before the Lord," referring to the place where incense was offered and holy bread was set out. Because it is made of wood rather than metal for burning animals, it points to prayer, thanksgiving, and peaceful fellowship with God.

differ.view: Calling the altar a table indicates that under the gospel, the bloody sacrifice is finished and believers now feast spiritually at the Lord's table.

notes.meaning: Both the outer sanctuary and the Most Holy Place have double doors to close their entrances. Each door is made of two folding panels that swing on hinges. This design allowed the priests to open the doors partly or fully as needed during sacred worship.

The wooden doors of the sanctuary are carved with cherubim and palm trees, matching the inner walls. Outside, the entrance porch features a wooden canopy overhead, along with narrow windows and carved palm trees on its sidewalls. The holy cherubim are kept inside the temple rooms, reminding worshippers that God's special presence is set apart from the outer world.
